name: Numerical methods
title: Numerical methods, one idea at a time
intro:
Numerical methods are the recipes computers use to get numbers out of maths that has no neat formula: the root of an equation, the area under a curve, the solution of a system of equations. This track explains each method in plain words, shows why it works and when it fails, and then implements it in several languages side by side, so you can compare how Python, C and Fortran say the same thing. Every implementation is tested against known values, and the versions in different languages must print the same answer. It assumes you can already write loops and functions in at least one of the languages. Topics arrive one at a time, starting with floating-point numbers and root finding.

Further reading: W. H. Press, S. A. Teukolsky, W. T. Vetterling and B. P. Flannery, Numerical Recipes: The Art of Scientific Computing, 3rd edition, Cambridge University Press, 2007, covers these topics and many more in depth. The explanations and code in this track are our own and are not taken from that book.

lessons.title: Floating-point numbers
lessons.summary: Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, machine epsilon, and comparing with a tolerance.

sections.p: Almost every numerical method works on floating-point numbers: the float in Python, double in C and real(real64) in Fortran. They store a number in binary with about 16 significant decimal digits. Most decimal fractions, such as 0.1, have no exact binary form, so they are stored as the nearest value that fits, and small errors creep into every result. Printing more digits than usual shows the error.

Machine epsilon is the gap between 1 and the next number a double can hold, about 2.2 × 10−16. It sets the best relative accuracy you can hope for: answers are only ever right to roughly 15 or 16 significant digits. Adding something much smaller than epsilon to 1 changes nothing at all.

sections.code:
import sys
eps = sys.float_info.epsilon
print(f"{eps:.3e}")
print(1.0 + eps / 4 == 1.0)

program eps
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  real(real64) :: e
  e = epsilon(1.0_real64)
  print '(es10.3)', e
  print '(l1)', 1.0_real64 + e / 4 == 1.0_real64
end program eps

sections.p: Because of these errors, never test two computed floats with ==. Check that they are close instead: abs(a - b) < tol, where the tolerance suits the size of the numbers. The methods in this track stop the same way, when a change gets smaller than a tolerance you choose.
sections.code:
a = 0.1 + 0.2
tol = 1e-12
print(abs(a - 0.3) < tol)

practice.q: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 come out false?
options: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so small errors add up
0.3 is too big for a double
practice.answer: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so small errors add up
practice.why: Each value is stored as the nearest binary fraction, and the tiny errors make the sum differ from the stored 0.3 in the last digit.

practice.q: About how many significant decimal digits does a double hold?
practice.why: A 64-bit double has a 53-bit mantissa, which is a little under 16 decimal digits. A 32-bit float has about 7.

practice.q: What does this print?
practice.answer: True
practice.why: The difference is about 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁷, far below the tolerance.

practice.q: How should you check that two computed doubles a and b are equal?
options: abs(a - b) < tol, with a suitable tolerance
practice.answer: abs(a - b) < tol, with a suitable tolerance
practice.why: Computed values carry rounding errors, so exact equality fails when the maths says they should match.

lessons.title: Root finding: bisection
lessons.summary: Halving an interval that brackets a sign change.

sections.p: A root of a function f is a value x where f(x) = 0. Finding √2, for example, is finding the root of f(x) = x² − 2. Many equations have no formula for their roots, so we search for them.

If f is continuous and f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, the curve must cross zero somewhere between a and b; the interval brackets a root. Look at the midpoint m. Whichever half still has a sign change keeps the root, so throw the other half away and repeat. Each step halves the interval, so after n steps it is (b − a) / 2n wide. Shrinking a width of 1 below 10−12 takes 40 steps, because 240 is just over 1012.

Bisection always works once you have a bracket, and you know in advance how many steps it will take. It is slow, gaining one binary digit per step, and it needs a sign change, so it cannot find a root where the curve only touches zero, such as x² = 0. Below, the same function finds √2 and the root of cos x = x (about 0.739, the number you get by pressing cos over and over on a calculator).

sections.code:
import math

def bisect(f, a, b, tol=1e-12):
    fa = f(a)
    if fa * f(b) > 0:
        raise ValueError("f(a) and f(b) must have opposite signs")
    steps = 0
    while b - a > tol:
        m = (a + b) / 2
        fm = f(m)
        if fa * fm <= 0:    # the sign change is in [a, m]
            b = m
        else:               # the sign change is in [m, b]
            a, fa = m, fm
        steps += 1
    return (a + b) / 2, steps

root, steps = bisect(lambda x: x * x - 2, 1.0, 2.0)
print(f"{root:.10f} after {steps} steps")
root, steps = bisect(lambda x: math.cos(x) - x, 0.0, 1.0)
print(f"{root:.10f} after {steps} steps")

sections.p: In C the function is passed as a pointer, and the step count comes back through a pointer argument.
In Fortran an abstract interface describes the kind of function bisect accepts, and procedure(fn) declares the argument.
sections.code:
program bisection
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  abstract interface
    function fn(x) result(y)
      import :: real64
      real(real64), intent(in) :: x
      real(real64) :: y
    end function fn
  end interface
  real(real64) :: root
  integer :: steps

  call bisect(square_minus_two, 1.0_real64, 2.0_real64, 1.0e-12_real64, root, steps)
  print '(f12.10, a, i0, a)', root, ' after ', steps, ' steps'
  call bisect(cos_minus_x, 0.0_real64, 1.0_real64, 1.0e-12_real64, root, steps)
  print '(f12.10, a, i0, a)', root, ' after ', steps, ' steps'
contains
  subroutine bisect(f, a0, b0, tol, root, steps)
    procedure(fn) :: f
    real(real64), intent(in) :: a0, b0, tol
    real(real64), intent(out) :: root
    integer, intent(out) :: steps
    real(real64) :: a, b, m, fa, fm
    a = a0
    b = b0
    fa = f(a)
    steps = 0
    do while (b - a > tol)
      m = (a + b) / 2
      fm = f(m)
      if (fa * fm <= 0) then
        b = m
      else
        a = m
        fa = fm
      end if
      steps = steps + 1
    end do
    root = (a + b) / 2
  end subroutine bisect

  function square_minus_two(x) result(y)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: x
    real(real64) :: y
    y = x * x - 2
  end function square_minus_two

  function cos_minus_x(x) result(y)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: x
    real(real64) :: y
    y = cos(x) - x
  end function cos_minus_x
end program bisection

practice.q: What must be true of f(a) and f(b) before bisection can start?
practice.answer: They have opposite signs
practice.why: A sign change guarantees that a continuous function crosses zero between a and b.

practice.q: The interval starts 1 wide. How many bisection steps make it narrower than 0.001?
practice.why: After n steps the width is 1 / 2ⁿ, and 2¹⁰ = 1024 is the first power of two above 1000.

practice.q: Bisection on f(x) = x − 0.3 over [0, 1]. Which half is kept after the first step?
practice.code:
f = lambda x: x - 0.3
a, b = 0.0, 1.0
m = (a + b) / 2
if f(a) * f(m) <= 0:
    b = m
else:
    a = m
print(a, b)
practice.why: f(0) = −0.3 and f(0.5) = 0.2 have opposite signs, so the root is in the left half.

practice.q: Why can bisection not find the root of f(x) = x² at 0?
options: The function touches zero without changing sign
practice.answer: The function touches zero without changing sign
practice.why: x² is never negative, so no interval has a sign change for bisection to start from.

practice.q: What is bisection's main strength?
options: It finds every root at once
practice.answer: Once started, it always converges
practice.why: A bracket can only shrink around the root, so it cannot wander off. The cost is speed: one binary digit per step.

lessons.title: Root finding: Newton's method
lessons.summary: Following the tangent line, and why it is fast but fragile.

sections.p: Newton's method uses the slope as well as the value. At a guess x, draw the tangent line to the curve and see where it crosses zero; that crossing is the next guess. The tangent crosses at x − f(x) / f′(x), so each step is xnew = x − f(x) / f′(x). Stop when the step gets smaller than a tolerance.

Close to a simple root, Newton's method roughly doubles the number of correct digits each step (this is called quadratic convergence). For √2 with f(x) = x² − 2 and f′(x) = 2x, starting from 1, watch the correct digits grow: 1, 3, 6, then all of them. Bisection needed 40 steps for the same accuracy. (This particular case is also the old "divide and average" way of working out square roots by hand.)

sections.code:
program newton_demo
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  real(real64) :: x, dx
  integer :: step
  logical :: converged

  x = 1.0_real64
  converged = .false.
  do step = 1, 50
    dx = f(x) / df(x)
    x = x - dx
    print '(a, i0, a, f14.12)', 'step ', step, ': ', x
    if (abs(dx) < 1.0e-12_real64) then
      converged = .true.
      exit
    end if
  end do
  if (converged) then
    print '(a, f12.10)', 'root ', x
  else
    print '(a)', 'did not converge'
  end if
contains
  function f(x) result(y)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: x
    real(real64) :: y
    y = x * x - 2
  end function f

  function df(x) result(y)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: x
    real(real64) :: y
    y = 2 * x
  end function df
end program newton_demo

sections.p: Newton's method needs a good start. Where the slope is zero the step divides by zero, and where the slope is small the step can throw the guess far away. Some starting points make it bounce between two values forever. That is why real code always caps the number of steps, as max_steps does above, and why a common robust approach brackets the root first and uses Newton steps only while they stay inside the bracket, falling back to bisection otherwise. Newton's method also needs the derivative; when that is hard to write down, the secant method replaces it with the slope through the last two guesses.
x³ − 2x − 5 = 0 is a classic test equation; its real root is 2.0945514815… Starting from 2, Newton's method gets there in a handful of steps.

practice.q: What is one Newton step for f(x)?
practice.answer: x − f(x) / f′(x)
practice.why: It is where the tangent line at x crosses zero.

practice.q: One Newton step for f(x) = x² − 9, starting at x = 5. What does it print?
practice.code:
x = 5.0
x = x - (x * x - 9) / (2 * x)
print(x)
practice.why: f(5) = 16 and f′(5) = 10, so the step is 5 − 16 / 10 = 3.4. The next step lands near 3.02.

practice.q: Near a simple root, roughly what happens to the number of correct digits each Newton step?
practice.answer: It doubles
practice.why: That is quadratic convergence: the new error is about the square of the old one.

practice.q: Why does good Newton code limit the number of steps?
options: A bad start can make it wander or cycle forever
The answer gets worse after 50 steps
practice.answer: A bad start can make it wander or cycle forever
practice.why: Unlike bisection, Newton's method has no bracket to keep it near the root.

practice.q: What does the secant method use instead of the derivative?
options: The slope through the last two guesses
practice.answer: The slope through the last two guesses
practice.why: It needs no derivative formula, and still converges faster than bisection.

lessons.title: Integration: trapezoids and Simpson's rule
lessons.summary: Adding up thin slices to find the area under a curve, and how fast the error shrinks.

sections.p: The integral of f from a to b is the area under its curve. Many integrals have no formula, so we cut the interval into n thin slices of width h = (b − a) / n, estimate the area of each slice, and add them up. This is called quadrature.

Join the curve's values at the ends of each slice with a straight line, so each slice becomes a trapezoid with area h × (f(left) + f(right)) / 2. Adding them up, every inside point is counted twice and the two end points once, which gives h × (f(a)/2 + f(x1) + … + f(xn−1) + f(b)/2). The error shrinks like h²: twice as many slices make it about four times smaller.

Fit a parabola through each pair of slices instead of a straight line. That works out to the weights 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, …, 4, 1, times h/3, and needs an even number of slices. Its error shrinks like h⁴: twice as many slices make it about sixteen times smaller, for the same number of function evaluations. Below, both rules integrate sin x from 0 to π, whose exact area is 2. Each time n grows four times, the trapezoid error falls about 16 times and Simpson's about 256 times. The last line also finds π as the integral of 4 / (1 + x²) from 0 to 1.

sections.code:
import math

def trapezoid(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    total = (f(a) + f(b)) / 2
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += f(a + i * h)
    return total * h

def simpson(f, a, b, n):    # n must be even
    h = (b - a) / n
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        weight = 4 if i % 2 == 1 else 2
        total += weight * f(a + i * h)
    return total * h / 3

print("   n  trapezoid error  Simpson error")
for n in (4, 16, 64):
    t = abs(trapezoid(math.sin, 0.0, math.pi, n) - 2)
    s = abs(simpson(math.sin, 0.0, math.pi, n) - 2)
    print(f"{n:4d}  {t:.10f}     {s:.10f}")
area = simpson(math.sin, 0.0, math.pi, 256)
pi = simpson(lambda x: 4 / (1 + x * x), 0.0, 1.0, 256)
print(f"{area:.8f} {pi:.8f}")

sections.p: In C, sin from the maths library can be passed straight in as a function pointer. C has no π constant in the standard, so acos(-1.0) gives it.
Fortran can't pass the generic sin intrinsic as an argument, so a small sine function wraps it. i * h mixes an integer and a real, and Fortran converts the integer first, just as C and Python do.
sections.code:
program integration
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  abstract interface
    function fn(x) result(y)
      import :: real64
      real(real64), intent(in) :: x
      real(real64) :: y
    end function fn
  end interface
  real(real64), parameter :: pi = acos(-1.0_real64)
  integer, parameter :: sizes(3) = [4, 16, 64]
  real(real64) :: t, s
  integer :: k

  print '(a)', '   n  trapezoid error  Simpson error'
  do k = 1, 3
    t = abs(trapezoid(sine, 0.0_real64, pi, sizes(k)) - 2)
    s = abs(simpson(sine, 0.0_real64, pi, sizes(k)) - 2)
    print '(i4, 2x, f12.10, 5x, f12.10)', sizes(k), t, s
  end do
  print '(f10.8, 1x, f10.8)', simpson(sine, 0.0_real64, pi, 256), &
                              simpson(quarter_circle, 0.0_real64, 1.0_real64, 256)
contains
  function trapezoid(f, a, b, n) result(total)
    procedure(fn) :: f
    real(real64), intent(in) :: a, b
    integer, intent(in) :: n
    real(real64) :: h, total
    integer :: i
    h = (b - a) / n
    total = (f(a) + f(b)) / 2
    do i = 1, n - 1
      total = total + f(a + i * h)
    end do
    total = total * h
  end function trapezoid

  function simpson(f, a, b, n) result(total)   ! n must be even
    procedure(fn) :: f
    real(real64), intent(in) :: a, b
    integer, intent(in) :: n
    real(real64) :: h, total
    integer :: i, weight
    h = (b - a) / n
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    do i = 1, n - 1
      if (mod(i, 2) == 1) then
        weight = 4
      else
        weight = 2
      end if
      total = total + weight * f(a + i * h)
    end do
    total = total * h / 3
  end function simpson

  function sine(x) result(y)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: x
    real(real64) :: y
    y = sin(x)
  end function sine

  function quarter_circle(x) result(y)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: x
    real(real64) :: y
    y = 4 / (1 + x * x)
  end function quarter_circle
end program integration

sections.p: In practice you rarely know the error in advance. A common approach is to double n until two answers agree to the accuracy you need; with the trapezoid rule, each doubling can reuse every point already computed. Both rules assume a smooth function: a corner, a jump or an infinite value inside the interval spoils the error estimates, and the interval should be split at that point.

practice.q: With the trapezoid rule, you double the number of slices. Roughly what happens to the error?
practice.answer: It becomes about 4 times smaller
practice.why: The trapezoid error shrinks like h², and halving h divides h² by 4.

practice.q: What weights does Simpson's rule give the points, before multiplying by h/3?
practice.why: Each parabola over two slices weighs its ends 1 and its middle 4. Neighbouring parabolas share an end, which gives the inner 2s.

practice.q: Why does Simpson's rule need an even number of slices?
practice.answer: Each parabola covers two slices
practice.why: The slices are taken in pairs, one parabola per pair, so they must pair up exactly.

practice.q: The trapezoid rule with one slice on f(x) = x² from 0 to 2. What does it print?
practice.code:
f = lambda x: x * x
a, b = 0.0, 2.0
print((b - a) * (f(a) + f(b)) / 2)
practice.why: One trapezoid: width 2 times the average of f(0) = 0 and f(2) = 4. The true area is 8/3, so one slice overshoots badly.

lessons.title: Linear systems: Gaussian elimination
lessons.summary: Solving several equations at once by elimination, back substitution and pivoting.

sections.p: A linear system is a set of equations such as 2x + y − z = 8, where each unknown is only multiplied by a number and added. Written as a table of coefficients, it becomes Ax = b: the matrix A holds the numbers in front of the unknowns, x is the list of unknowns, and b is the right-hand sides. Systems like this are everywhere: circuits, structures, statistics, and inside most other numerical methods.

Take the first equation and subtract a multiple of it from every row below, chosen so that the first unknown disappears from them. Repeat with the second row on the rows below it, and so on. What is left is upper triangular: the last equation has one unknown, the one above it two, and so on. Solve the last equation, put that value into the one above, and work upwards. This is back substitution. For n equations elimination takes about n³/3 multiplications, so doubling the size makes it about eight times slower.

Each step divides by the number on the diagonal, the pivot. If the pivot is zero the method stops, and if it is merely tiny, the multipliers become huge and rounding errors swamp the answer. Partial pivoting fixes this cheaply: before clearing a column, swap in the row whose entry in that column is largest in size. Below, a system whose answer is almost exactly x = 1, y = 1 comes out completely wrong without the swap.
sections.code:
def solve2(A, b, pivot):
    A = [row[:] for row in A]
    b = b[:]
    if pivot and abs(A[1][0]) > abs(A[0][0]):
        A[0], A[1] = A[1], A[0]
        b[0], b[1] = b[1], b[0]
    m = A[1][0] / A[0][0]
    A[1][1] -= m * A[0][1]
    b[1] -= m * b[0]
    y = b[1] / A[1][1]
    x = (b[0] - A[0][1] * y) / A[0][0]
    return x, y

# 0.00000000000000000001 x + y = 1
#                      x + y = 2     (the answer is very close to x = 1, y = 1)
A = [[1e-20, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]]
b = [1.0, 2.0]
print("without pivoting:", solve2(A, b, pivot=False))
print("with pivoting:   ", solve2(A, b, pivot=True))

sections.p: Here is elimination with partial pivoting for any size, solving 2x + y − z = 8, −3x − y + 2z = −11, −2x + y + 2z = −3, whose answer is x = 2, y = 3, z = −1. The function works on copies so the caller's matrix is left alone.
sections.code:
def solve(A, b):
    n = len(b)
    A = [row[:] for row in A]   # work on copies
    b = b[:]
    for k in range(n):
        # Partial pivoting: bring the row with the largest entry in column k up to row k.
        p = max(range(k, n), key=lambda i: abs(A[i][k]))
        if A[p][k] == 0:
            raise ValueError("the matrix is singular")
        A[k], A[p] = A[p], A[k]
        b[k], b[p] = b[p], b[k]
        # Elimination: clear column k below the pivot.
        for i in range(k + 1, n):
            m = A[i][k] / A[k][k]
            for j in range(k, n):
                A[i][j] -= m * A[k][j]
            b[i] -= m * b[k]
    # Back substitution, from the last row up.
    x = [0.0] * n
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        s = b[i]
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            s -= A[i][j] * x[j]
        x[i] = s / A[i][i]
    return x

A = [[2.0, 1.0, -1.0],
     [-3.0, -1.0, 2.0],
     [-2.0, 1.0, 2.0]]
b = [8.0, -11.0, -3.0]
for i, value in enumerate(solve(A, b)):
    print(f"x{i + 1} = {value:.10f}")

sections.p: In C the size is fixed with #define to keep the code short, and the function reports a singular matrix by returning −1 rather than stopping the program.

Fortran was built for this kind of work. Whole rows can be swapped with array sections such as A(k, :), and maxloc finds the pivot. Fortran stores matrices column by column, so reshape takes the numbers a column at a time.
sections.code:
program linear_system
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 3
  real(real64) :: A(n, n), b(n), x(n)
  integer :: i

  ! Fortran fills arrays column by column, so reshape takes the columns.
  A = reshape([2.0_real64, -3.0_real64, -2.0_real64, &
               1.0_real64, -1.0_real64, 1.0_real64, &
               -1.0_real64, 2.0_real64, 2.0_real64], [n, n])
  b = [8.0_real64, -11.0_real64, -3.0_real64]
  call solve(A, b, x)
  do i = 1, n
    print '(a, i0, a, f0.10)', 'x', i, ' = ', x(i)
  end do
contains
  subroutine solve(A, b, x)
    real(real64), intent(inout) :: A(:, :), b(:)
    real(real64), intent(out) :: x(:)
    real(real64) :: row(size(b)), t, m, s
    integer :: k, p, i, j, n
    n = size(b)
    do k = 1, n
      ! Partial pivoting: the largest entry in column k, from row k down.
      p = k - 1 + maxloc(abs(A(k:n, k)), dim=1)
      if (A(p, k) == 0) error stop 'the matrix is singular'
      row = A(k, :)
      A(k, :) = A(p, :)
      A(p, :) = row
      t = b(k)
      b(k) = b(p)
      b(p) = t
      ! Elimination: clear column k below the pivot.
      do i = k + 1, n
        m = A(i, k) / A(k, k)
        do j = k, n
          A(i, j) = A(i, j) - m * A(k, j)
        end do
        b(i) = b(i) - m * b(k)
      end do
    end do
    ! Back substitution, from the last row up.
    do i = n, 1, -1
      s = b(i)
      do j = i + 1, n
        s = s - A(i, j) * x(j)
      end do
      x(i) = s / A(i, i)
    end do
  end subroutine solve
end program linear_system

sections.p: Writing elimination yourself is the best way to understand it, but for real work use a tested library such as LAPACK, which numpy.linalg.solve and most languages' maths libraries call underneath. They are faster and handle the awkward cases. Two warnings carry over to every library. A matrix can be singular (no unique answer) or nearly so (ill-conditioned), and then tiny changes in b cause huge changes in x. And to solve Ax = b, don't compute the inverse of A and multiply: elimination is cheaper and more accurate.

practice.q: What shape is the matrix after elimination, before back substitution?
options: Upper triangular: zeros below the diagonal
Diagonal: zeros everywhere off the diagonal
Lower triangular: zeros above the diagonal
practice.answer: Upper triangular: zeros below the diagonal
practice.why: Each step clears one column below the diagonal, so only the diagonal and the entries above it are left.

practice.q: Partial pivoting swaps rows so that the pivot is…
options: the largest in size in its column, from the current row down
the first entry of the row
practice.answer: the largest in size in its column, from the current row down
practice.why: A large pivot keeps the multipliers at 1 or below, so rounding errors can't grow out of control.

practice.q: Solving a 100-equation system takes 1 second. Roughly how long does a 200-equation system take?
practice.answer: 8 seconds
practice.why: Elimination costs about n³/3 operations, and 2³ = 8.

practice.q: Back substitution on 2x + y = 7 and 3y = 9. What does it print?
practice.why: The last equation gives y = 3; putting it into the first gives 2x = 4, so x = 2.

lessons.title: Interpolation: Newton's divided differences
lessons.summary: Fitting one polynomial through given points, evaluating it quickly, and why more points can make it worse.

sections.p: Often a function is known only at some points: measurements, a table, or values that are expensive to compute. Interpolation finds a function that passes exactly through those points, so you can estimate the values in between. The classic choice is a polynomial: through n + 1 points with different x values there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n.

Newton writes that polynomial as c0 + c1(x − x0) + c2(x − x0)(x − x1) + …. The coefficients are divided differences: c1 is the slope between the first two points, c2 is how fast that slope changes, and so on, each built from the level before. They fit in a single list that is updated in place. Adding a new point only adds one new coefficient, and the polynomial can be evaluated by nesting, like Horner's rule, with one multiplication per coefficient.

Below, four points come from x² + x + 1, though the code is never told that. The coefficients come out as 1, 2, 1 and 0. The last one is zero because the points really lie on a parabola, so the interpolating polynomial is that parabola, and its values in between are exact: p(3) = 13 and p(2.5) = 9.75.
sections.code:
def divided_differences(xs, ys):
    """Returns Newton's coefficients c0, c1, ... for the points (xs, ys)."""
    n = len(xs)
    c = ys[:]
    for level in range(1, n):
        # Work from the bottom up so each c[i] still holds the previous level.
        for i in range(n - 1, level - 1, -1):
            c[i] = (c[i] - c[i - 1]) / (xs[i] - xs[i - level])
    return c

def newton_value(xs, c, x):
    """Evaluates c0 + c1(x - x0) + c2(x - x0)(x - x1) + ... by nesting."""
    result = c[-1]
    for i in range(len(c) - 2, -1, -1):
        result = result * (x - xs[i]) + c[i]
    return result

xs = [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0]
ys = [1.0, 3.0, 7.0, 21.0]      # from x*x + x + 1, but the code doesn't know that
c = divided_differences(xs, ys)
print("coefficients:", " ".join(f"{v:.6f}" for v in c))
for x in (3.0, 2.5):
    print(f"p({x:.1f}) = {newton_value(xs, c, x):.6f}")

sections.p: In C the coefficients overwrite the array of y values, which is how the method is usually written when memory matters.
In Fortran the arrays start at 1, so the loops run one higher. Assumed-shape arguments such as xs(:) let the same routines work for any number of points.
sections.code:
program interpolation
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  real(real64) :: xs(4), c(4), points(2)
  integer :: k

  xs = [0.0_real64, 1.0_real64, 2.0_real64, 4.0_real64]
  c = [1.0_real64, 3.0_real64, 7.0_real64, 21.0_real64]   ! from x*x + x + 1
  call divided_differences(xs, c)
  print '(a, 4(1x, f8.6))', 'coefficients:', c
  points = [3.0_real64, 2.5_real64]
  do k = 1, 2
    print '(a, f3.1, a, f0.6)', 'p(', points(k), ') = ', newton_value(xs, c, points(k))
  end do
contains
  ! Replaces c (which starts as the y values) with Newton's coefficients.
  subroutine divided_differences(xs, c)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: xs(:)
    real(real64), intent(inout) :: c(:)
    integer :: level, i, n
    n = size(xs)
    do level = 1, n - 1
      do i = n, level + 1, -1
        c(i) = (c(i) - c(i - 1)) / (xs(i) - xs(i - level))
      end do
    end do
  end subroutine divided_differences

  ! Evaluates the Newton form by nesting, from the last coefficient back.
  function newton_value(xs, c, x) result(total)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: xs(:), c(:), x
    real(real64) :: total
    integer :: i
    total = c(size(c))
    do i = size(c) - 1, 1, -1
      total = total * (x - xs(i)) + c(i)
    end do
  end function newton_value
end program interpolation

sections.h: More points is not always better
sections.p: It seems that more points must give a better fit, but with equally spaced points a high-degree polynomial can swing wildly near the ends of the interval. This is called Runge's phenomenon, after Carl Runge, who showed it with 1 / (1 + 25x²) on [−1, 1]. The cure is to bunch the points towards the ends: Chebyshev points, cos((2i + 1)π / (2n + 2)), keep the error small as n grows. In practice it is often better still to use many low-degree pieces joined smoothly, called splines, rather than one high-degree polynomial.
sections.code:
import math

def interpolate(xs, ys, x):
    """Lagrange form: the sum of ys[i] times a polynomial that is 1 at xs[i] and 0 at the others."""
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(len(xs)):
        term = ys[i]
        for j in range(len(xs)):
            if j != i:
                term *= (x - xs[j]) / (xs[i] - xs[j])
        total += term
    return total

f = lambda x: 1 / (1 + 25 * x * x)
test = [-1 + k / 500 for k in range(1001)]
for n in (5, 10, 20):
    even = [-1 + 2 * i / n for i in range(n + 1)]
    cheb = [math.cos((2 * i + 1) * math.pi / (2 * n + 2)) for i in range(n + 1)]
    worst_even = max(abs(interpolate(even, [f(x) for x in even], t) - f(t)) for t in test)
    worst_cheb = max(abs(interpolate(cheb, [f(x) for x in cheb], t) - f(t)) for t in test)
    print(f"{n + 1:2d} points: equally spaced {worst_even:6.2f}, Chebyshev {worst_cheb:4.2f}")
sections.out:
6 points: equally spaced   0.43, Chebyshev 0.56
11 points: equally spaced   1.92, Chebyshev 0.11
21 points: equally spaced  59.77, Chebyshev 0.02

practice.q: Through how many points does a polynomial of degree 3 pass, in general?
practice.why: A degree-3 polynomial has four coefficients, so four points fix it.

practice.q: The highest divided difference of some points comes out exactly 0. What does that tell you?
options: The points lie on a polynomial of lower degree
practice.answer: The points lie on a polynomial of lower degree
practice.why: The last coefficient multiplies the highest power, so if it's 0 a lower-degree polynomial already fits every point.

practice.q: Interpolating 1 / (1 + 25x²) at 21 equally spaced points gives huge errors near ±1. What helps most?
options: Using Chebyshev points, bunched towards the ends
Using even more equally spaced points
Using Newton's form instead of Lagrange's
practice.answer: Using Chebyshev points, bunched towards the ends
practice.why: The swings come from where the points are placed, not from rounding or the form of the polynomial; more equally spaced points make it worse.

practice.q: The first divided difference between (1, 4) and (3, 10). What does it print?
practice.why: It is the slope between the points: a rise of 6 over a run of 2.

lessons.title: Differential equations: Euler and Runge–Kutta
lessons.summary: Following a quantity through time from the rule for how fast it changes.

sections.p: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) gives the rate of change of something in terms of its current value and the time: y′ = f(t, y). A population that grows in proportion to its size obeys y′ = y; a cooling cup of tea obeys y′ = −k(y − room temperature). Given a starting value y(t0), we want y at later times. Most ODEs have no formula for the answer, so we step forward in small time steps of size h.

The simplest step uses the slope at the start of the step as if it stayed the same: ynew = y + h f(t, y). It is easy to understand but crude. Its error is proportional to h, so halving the step only halves the error, and getting six correct digits can take a million steps.

RK4, from Carl Runge and Wilhelm Kutta around 1900, samples the slope four times per step: at the start (k1), twice at the middle (k2 and k3, each using the slope just found), and at the end (k4). It then moves with the weighted average (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4) / 6. Its error is proportional to h⁴, so halving the step makes it 16 times smaller. Below, both methods solve y′ = y with y(0) = 1 up to t = 1, where the exact answer is e. Each time the number of steps doubles, Euler's error halves while RK4's drops 16 times, even though RK4 does four times the work per step.
sections.code:
import math

def euler(f, t, y, h, steps):
    for _ in range(steps):
        y = y + h * f(t, y)
        t = t + h
    return y

def rk4(f, t, y, h, steps):
    for _ in range(steps):
        k1 = f(t, y)
        k2 = f(t + h / 2, y + h / 2 * k1)
        k3 = f(t + h / 2, y + h / 2 * k2)
        k4 = f(t + h, y + h * k3)
        y = y + h / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)
        t = t + h
    return y

growth = lambda t, y: y        # y' = y with y(0) = 1, so y(1) = e
print("  steps  Euler error   RK4 error")
for steps in (10, 20, 40):
    h = 1.0 / steps
    e1 = abs(euler(growth, 0.0, 1.0, h, steps) - math.e)
    e4 = abs(rk4(growth, 0.0, 1.0, h, steps) - math.e)
    print(f"{steps:7d}  {e1:.10f}  {e4:.10f}")
print(f"RK4 with 100 steps: {rk4(growth, 0.0, 1.0, 0.01, 100):.8f}")

sections.p: In C the right-hand side f(t, y) is passed as a function pointer, just as in the root-finding lessons. (void)t; tells the compiler that ignoring t is deliberate.
In Fortran an abstract interface describes the right-hand side, and the step size and number of steps are passed in, so the same routines work for any equation.
sections.code:
program odes
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  abstract interface
    function deriv(t, y) result(dy)
      import :: real64
      real(real64), intent(in) :: t, y
      real(real64) :: dy
    end function deriv
  end interface
  real(real64), parameter :: e = exp(1.0_real64)
  integer, parameter :: sizes(3) = [10, 20, 40]
  real(real64) :: h, e1, e4
  integer :: k

  print '(a)', '  steps  Euler error   RK4 error'
  do k = 1, 3
    h = 1.0_real64 / sizes(k)
    e1 = abs(euler(growth, 0.0_real64, 1.0_real64, h, sizes(k)) - e)
    e4 = abs(rk4(growth, 0.0_real64, 1.0_real64, h, sizes(k)) - e)
    print '(i7, 2x, f12.10, 2x, f12.10)', sizes(k), e1, e4
  end do
  print '(a, f10.8)', 'RK4 with 100 steps: ', rk4(growth, 0.0_real64, 1.0_real64, 0.01_real64, 100)
contains
  function euler(f, t0, y0, h, steps) result(y)
    procedure(deriv) :: f
    real(real64), intent(in) :: t0, y0, h
    integer, intent(in) :: steps
    real(real64) :: t, y
    integer :: i
    t = t0
    y = y0
    do i = 1, steps
      y = y + h * f(t, y)
      t = t + h
    end do
  end function euler

  function rk4(f, t0, y0, h, steps) result(y)
    procedure(deriv) :: f
    real(real64), intent(in) :: t0, y0, h
    integer, intent(in) :: steps
    real(real64) :: t, y, k1, k2, k3, k4
    integer :: i
    t = t0
    y = y0
    do i = 1, steps
      k1 = f(t, y)
      k2 = f(t + h / 2, y + h / 2 * k1)
      k3 = f(t + h / 2, y + h / 2 * k2)
      k4 = f(t + h, y + h * k3)
      y = y + h / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)
      t = t + h
    end do
  end function rk4

  ! y' = y with y(0) = 1, so y(1) = e
  function growth(t, y) result(dy)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: t, y
    real(real64) :: dy
    dy = y
  end function growth
end program odes

sections.p: The same steps work for several quantities at once: make y a list (a vector) and f return a list of rates, such as predators and prey that depend on each other. A second-order equation such as a swinging pendulum, θ″ = −(g/L) sin θ, becomes two first-order ones by tracking both the angle and its speed. Real solvers, such as scipy.integrate.solve_ivp, also change h as they go, taking big steps where the solution is smooth and small ones where it changes fast. Some equations, called stiff, mix very fast and very slow changes, and need special implicit methods to stay stable.

practice.q: With Euler's method you halve the step size. Roughly what happens to the error at the end?
practice.answer: It halves
practice.why: Euler's error is proportional to h, so it shrinks in step with h.

practice.q: How many times does RK4 evaluate f in each step?
practice.why: k1 at the start, k2 and k3 at the middle, and k4 at the end.

practice.q: How do you solve a second-order equation such as θ″ = −sin θ with these methods?
options: Track θ and θ′ together as a pair of first-order equations
Apply Euler twice in a row
practice.answer: Track θ and θ′ together as a pair of first-order equations
practice.why: θ′ = ω and ω′ = −sin θ is a first-order system, and the methods work on vectors as well as single numbers.

practice.q: One Euler step of y′ = 2y from y(0) = 3 with h = 0.5. What does it print?
practice.code:
y, h = 3.0, 0.5
y = y + h * (2 * y)
print(y)
practice.why: The slope at the start is 2 × 3 = 6, and moving for 0.5 adds 3.

lessons.title: Minimization: golden-section search
lessons.summary: Finding the lowest point of a function by squeezing a bracket around it.

sections.p: Many problems ask for the input that makes something as small as possible: the cheapest design, the shortest path, the model that fits data with the least error. For a function of one variable, f(x), we want the x where f is lowest. Root finding looked for where f crosses zero; here we look for where it bottoms out. The function below, f(x) = x² − 4 sin x, dips to a minimum somewhere between 0 and 3.

Bisection trapped a root between two points where f had opposite signs. A minimum needs three points instead: a < c < b with f(c) lower than both ends, which guarantees a dip in between (for a function without jumps). To shrink the bracket we try a fourth point d inside it. If f(c) < f(d), the minimum is in [a, d]; otherwise it is in [c, b]. Either way one end is cut off and a lower inner point remains.

Where should the inner points go? If they sit at fractions 0.382 and 0.618 of the way across the bracket, then after cutting, the surviving inner point lands exactly at 0.382 or 0.618 of the new, smaller bracket. So each step reuses one old value and needs only one new evaluation of f, and the bracket shrinks by the same factor 0.618 every time. That number is (√5 − 1)/2, the golden ratio minus one, which gives the method its name. Starting from a bracket 3 wide, 41 steps bring it below 10⁻⁸, since 3 × 0.618⁴¹ ≈ 10⁻⁸.
sections.code:
import math

R = (math.sqrt(5) - 1) / 2   # 0.618..., the golden ratio minus one


def golden(f, a, b, tol):
    c = b - R * (b - a)
    d = a + R * (b - a)
    fc, fd = f(c), f(d)
    steps = 0
    while b - a > tol:
        if fc < fd:          # the minimum is in [a, d]
            b, d, fd = d, c, fc
            c = b - R * (b - a)
            fc = f(c)
        else:                # the minimum is in [c, b]
            a, c, fc = c, d, fd
            d = a + R * (b - a)
            fd = f(d)
        steps += 1
    return (a + b) / 2, steps


def f(x):
    return x * x - 4 * math.sin(x)


x, steps = golden(f, 0.0, 3.0, 1e-8)
print(f"{steps} steps")
print(f"minimum at x = {x:.8f}")
print(f"f(x) = {f(x):.8f}")

sections.p: The C version passes the function as a pointer and returns the number of steps through a pointer argument, since a C function can only return one value.
In Fortran an abstract interface describes the function to minimize, and steps is an intent(out) argument. The edit descriptors print the same digits as the other two versions.
sections.code:
module minimize
  implicit none
  abstract interface
    function func(x) result(y)
      double precision, intent(in) :: x
      double precision :: y
    end function func
  end interface
contains
  ! Golden-section search for a minimum of f in [a, b].
  function golden(f, a0, b0, tol, steps) result(x)
    procedure(func) :: f
    double precision, intent(in) :: a0, b0, tol
    integer, intent(out) :: steps
    double precision :: x, a, b, c, d, fc, fd, r
    r = (sqrt(5d0) - 1d0) / 2d0
    a = a0
    b = b0
    c = b - r * (b - a)
    d = a + r * (b - a)
    fc = f(c)
    fd = f(d)
    steps = 0
    do while (b - a > tol)
      if (fc < fd) then        ! the minimum is in [a, d]
        b = d
        d = c
        fd = fc
        c = b - r * (b - a)
        fc = f(c)
      else                     ! the minimum is in [c, b]
        a = c
        c = d
        fc = fd
        d = a + r * (b - a)
        fd = f(d)
      end if
      steps = steps + 1
    end do
    x = (a + b) / 2
  end function golden

  function f(x) result(y)
    double precision, intent(in) :: x
    double precision :: y
    y = x * x - 4 * sin(x)
  end function f
end module minimize

program main
  use minimize
  implicit none
  integer :: steps
  double precision :: x
  x = golden(f, 0d0, 3d0, 1d-8, steps)
  print '(i0, a)', steps, ' steps'
  print '(a, f10.8)', 'minimum at x = ', x
  print '(a, f11.8)', 'f(x) = ', f(x)
end program main

sections.p: We stopped at a bracket of 10⁻⁸, not 10⁻¹⁶, and that is not laziness. Near a minimum a smooth function is shaped like a parabola, so moving a distance δ away only raises f by about δ². A step of 10⁻⁸ raises it by about 10⁻¹⁶, which is at the limit of what a double can tell apart from f itself (see the floating point lesson). Below that, comparing f(c) with f(d) is just comparing rounding errors. So a minimum can only be located to about the square root of the machine precision, roughly 8 digits, while its value f(x) is still good to nearly full precision.
sections.out:
step 1e-02 away: f grows by 2.7e-04
step 1e-04 away: f grows by 2.7e-08
step 1e-06 away: f grows by 2.7e-12
step 1e-08 away: f grows by 8.9e-16

sections.p: Golden-section search is slow but cannot fail once the minimum is bracketed. Brent's method speeds it up by fitting a parabola through the three points and jumping to its lowest point, falling back to a golden step when the parabola misbehaves; this is what scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar uses. If you can compute the derivative, you can instead find the root of f′ with Newton's method. With many variables, methods follow the downhill direction (gradient descent, the workhorse of machine learning) or move a small shape of points around (Nelder–Mead). All of these find a local minimum, the bottom of the nearest valley; finding the lowest point overall, the global minimum, is much harder and usually means trying many starting points.

practice.q: How many points does a bracket around a minimum need?
options: Three, with the middle one lowest
practice.answer: Three, with the middle one lowest
practice.why: If f(c) is below f(a) and f(b), the function must dip somewhere between a and b.

practice.q: By what factor does golden-section search shrink the bracket each step?
practice.answer: About 0.618
practice.why: The inner points are placed so that each step keeps 0.618 of the bracket and reuses one old point.

practice.q: Why can a minimum only be located to about 8 digits in double precision?
options: Near the minimum f changes by only about δ², which disappears in rounding below δ ≈ 10⁻⁸
Golden-section search always stops after 41 steps
practice.answer: Near the minimum f changes by only about δ², which disappears in rounding below δ ≈ 10⁻⁸
practice.why: The function is flat at the bottom, so differences in x of 10⁻⁸ give differences in f near 10⁻¹⁶, the limit of double precision.

practice.q: One golden-section step on f(x) = (x − 1)² with a = 0, b = 4. Which bracket is left?

a, b = 0.0, 4.0
c, d = b - r * (b - a), a + r * (b - a)
f = lambda x: (x - 1) ** 2
if f(c) < f(d):
    b = d
else:
    a = c
print(round(a, 3), round(b, 3))

lessons.title: Random numbers and Monte Carlo
lessons.summary: How a computer makes numbers that look random, how to test one, and using them to estimate π.

sections.p: Computers follow instructions exactly, so they can't produce true randomness on their own. Instead, a pseudo-random number generator keeps a hidden number, its state, and each call scrambles the state into a new one and hands out the result. The sequence looks random but is completely determined by the starting state, the seed. That is a feature: a simulation started from the same seed gives exactly the same results, which makes bugs repeatable.

The oldest kind multiplies the state by a constant and keeps the remainder: state ← a × state mod m. With m = 2³¹ − 1 (a prime) and a = 16807, every state from 1 to m − 1 appears once before the sequence repeats. Stephen Park and Keith Miller proposed this in 1988 as a minimal standard, and published a check: starting from 1, the 10000th state must be 1043618065. Dividing the state by m gives a number between 0 and 1. Because the generator uses only whole-number arithmetic, every language gives exactly the same sequence, so the same check works everywhere.

Monte Carlo methods, named after the casino, answer questions by random sampling. Throw random points into the unit square: the fraction that lands inside the quarter circle x² + y² < 1 is about π/4. The error shrinks only like 1/√N, so 100 times more points buy just one more correct digit. For a smooth one-dimensional integral the methods in the integration lesson are far better, but for integrals in many dimensions Monte Carlo is often the only practical method.
sections.code:
M = 2147483647      # 2**31 - 1, a prime
A = 16807           # 7**5, the "minimal standard" multiplier

def next_state(state):
    return A * state % M

# The published check: starting from 1, the 10000th state is 1043618065.
state = 1
for _ in range(10000):
    state = next_state(state)
print(f"state after 10000 steps: {state}, as a fraction {state / M:.10f}")

# Monte Carlo: the fraction of random points in the unit square that land
# inside the quarter circle x*x + y*y < 1 is about pi / 4.
inside = 0
trials = 100000
for _ in range(trials):
    state = next_state(state)
    x = state / M
    state = next_state(state)
    y = state / M
    if x * x + y * y < 1:
        inside += 1
print(f"pi is about {4 * inside / trials:.4f}")
sections.out:
state after 10000 steps: 1043618065, as a fraction 0.4859725318
pi is about 3.1406

sections.p: In C, a × state can be as large as about 2⁴⁵, which overflows a 32-bit int, so the state is an int64_t. Python's integers never overflow, so it needs no such care.
sections.out:
state after 10000 steps: 1043618065, as a fraction 0.4859725318
pi is about 3.1406

sections.p: Fortran asks for a 64-bit integer kind with int64 from iso_fortran_env, and real(state, real64) converts it to a double before dividing.
sections.code:
program random_numbers
  use iso_fortran_env, only: int64, real64
  implicit none
  integer(int64), parameter :: m = 2147483647_int64   ! 2**31 - 1, a prime
  integer(int64), parameter :: a = 16807_int64        ! 7**5, the "minimal standard" multiplier
  integer(int64) :: state
  real(real64) :: x, y
  integer :: i, inside
  integer, parameter :: trials = 100000

  ! The published check: starting from 1, the 10000th state is 1043618065.
  state = 1
  do i = 1, 10000
    state = next_state(state)
  end do
  print '(a, i0, a, f12.10)', 'state after 10000 steps: ', state, ', as a fraction ', &
        real(state, real64) / m

  ! Monte Carlo: points in the unit square inside the quarter circle.
  inside = 0
  do i = 1, trials
    state = next_state(state)
    x = real(state, real64) / m
    state = next_state(state)
    y = real(state, real64) / m
    if (x * x + y * y < 1) inside = inside + 1
  end do
  print '(a, f6.4)', 'pi is about ', 4.0_real64 * inside / trials
contains
  ! a * state can reach about 2**45, so it needs a 64-bit integer.
  function next_state(s) result(n)
    integer(int64), intent(in) :: s
    integer(int64) :: n
    n = mod(a * s, m)
  end function next_state
end program random_numbers

sections.p: The minimal standard is good for learning and for checking code, but it is weak by modern standards: its period of about two billion is used up in seconds, and neighbouring values are related in ways careful tests can detect. Use your language's library instead. Python's random uses the Mersenne Twister, and newer generators such as PCG and xoshiro are fast and pass much stronger tests. None of these are safe for passwords or keys, because their next output can be predicted from earlier ones; for that use a cryptographic source such as Python's secrets module.

practice.q: Two runs of a simulation use the same pseudo-random generator and the same seed. What happens?
options: They produce exactly the same numbers
practice.answer: They produce exactly the same numbers
practice.why: The sequence is fully determined by the seed, which is what makes runs repeatable.

practice.q: A Monte Carlo estimate with 10,000 points has an error of about 0.01. Roughly how many points bring it down to 0.001?
practice.why: The error falls like 1/√N, so a tenth of the error needs 100 times as many points.

practice.q: Which of these should you use to make a password?
options: A cryptographic source such as Python's secrets module
Any generator, seeded with the time
practice.answer: A cryptographic source such as Python's secrets module
practice.why: Ordinary generators are predictable from their earlier outputs; cryptographic sources are designed not to be.

state = 1
for _ in range(3):

lessons.title: Eigenvalues: power iteration
lessons.summary: Finding the direction a matrix stretches most, by multiplying again and again.

sections.p: Multiplying a vector by a matrix usually turns it and stretches it. But for most square matrices there are special directions that only get stretched: Av = λv. Such a v is an eigenvector and the stretch factor λ is its eigenvalue. They describe how a system behaves on its own: the ways a bridge or a guitar string vibrates and at what frequencies, which web pages a random surfer ends up on (the idea behind PageRank), and the main directions of variation in a cloud of data points.

Start with almost any vector and keep multiplying it by A. Each multiplication stretches the part along each eigenvector by that eigenvector's eigenvalue, so the part with the largest eigenvalue (in size) grows fastest and soon dominates. Dividing by the vector's length after each step stops the numbers from overflowing. Once the direction settles, the stretch tells us the eigenvalue. For a symmetric matrix the best estimate is the Rayleigh quotient v · Av, which is accurate to twice as many digits as the direction itself. The matrix below, with 2 on the diagonal and −1 beside it, describes a chain of three masses joined by springs; its largest eigenvalue is 2 + √2.
sections.code:
import math

A = [[2.0, -1.0, 0.0],
     [-1.0, 2.0, -1.0],
     [0.0, -1.0, 2.0]]


def times(A, v):
    return [sum(A[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(A))]


def dot(u, v):
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))


v = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
estimate = 0.0
for step in range(1, 101):
    w = times(A, v)
    new = dot(v, w)                      # Rayleigh quotient, since v has length 1
    size = math.sqrt(dot(w, w))
    v = [x / size for x in w]
    if step in (1, 2, 5, 10, 20):
        print(f"step {step:2d}: {new:.10f}")
    if abs(new - estimate) < 1e-13:
        break
    estimate = new
print(f"after {step} steps the largest eigenvalue is {new:.10f}")
print("eigenvector:" + "".join(f"{x:10.6f}" for x in v))

sections.p: In C the matrix is a fixed-size two-dimensional array, and the result vector is passed in for the function to fill, since C functions cannot return arrays.

Fortran has whole-array operations, so v = w / size divides every element at once. It also has matmul and dot_product built in; we write the loops out here so the sums happen in exactly the same order as in Python and C, and the three print identical digits.
sections.code:
program power
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 3
  double precision :: a(n, n), v(n), w(n), estimate, now, size
  integer :: step
  ! Fortran fills arrays column by column; A is symmetric, so it reads the same.
  a = reshape([2d0, -1d0, 0d0, -1d0, 2d0, -1d0, 0d0, -1d0, 2d0], [n, n])
  v = [1d0, 0d0, 0d0]
  estimate = 0d0
  do step = 1, 100
    w = times(a, v)
    now = dot(v, w)              ! Rayleigh quotient, since v has length 1
    size = sqrt(dot(w, w))
    v = w / size
    if (any(step == [1, 2, 5, 10, 20])) print '(a, i2, a, f12.10)', 'step ', step, ': ', now
    if (abs(now - estimate) < 1d-13) exit
    estimate = now
  end do
  print '(a, i0, a, f12.10)', 'after ', step, ' steps the largest eigenvalue is ', now
  print '(a, 3f10.6)', 'eigenvector:', v
contains
  ! w = A v, with the sums in the same order as the other languages
  function times(a, v) result(w)
    double precision, intent(in) :: a(n, n), v(n)
    double precision :: w(n)
    integer :: i, j
    do i = 1, n
      w(i) = 0d0
      do j = 1, n
        w(i) = w(i) + a(i, j) * v(j)
      end do
    end do
  end function times

  function dot(u, v) result(s)
    double precision, intent(in) :: u(n), v(n)
    double precision :: s
    integer :: i
    s = 0d0
    do i = 1, n
      s = s + u(i) * v(i)
    end do
  end function dot
end program power

sections.p: Each step shrinks the unwanted part by the ratio of the second-largest eigenvalue to the largest. When the two are far apart that ratio is small and a few dozen steps are enough; when they are close, the method crawls. In this demo the largest eigenvalue is always 3 and only the second one changes.
sections.code:
import math


def steps_needed(second):
    # A = [[3, 0], [0, second]] has eigenvalues 3 and second
    v = [1.0, 1.0]
    for step in range(1, 100000):
        w = [3 * v[0], second * v[1]]
        size = math.sqrt(w[0] ** 2 + w[1] ** 2)
        v = [w[0] / size, w[1] / size]
        if abs(v[1]) < 1e-10:            # the second direction has died out
            return step


for second in [1.0, 2.0, 2.7, 2.97]:
    print(f"eigenvalues 3 and {second}: {steps_needed(second)} steps")

sections.p: Two small changes reach the other eigenvalues. Inverse iteration multiplies by A−1 instead (in practice, solving a linear system each step, as in the linear systems lesson), which finds the eigenvalue smallest in size. Shifting first, by working with A − σI, finds the eigenvalue closest to any guess σ, and updating σ from the Rayleigh quotient each step converges extremely fast. To get every eigenvalue at once, libraries use the QR algorithm (or Jacobi rotations for small symmetric matrices); in Python that is numpy.linalg.eigh for symmetric matrices and numpy.linalg.eig otherwise, both built on LAPACK.

practice.q: What does A v = λ v say about the vector v?
options: Multiplying by A only stretches v, without turning it
v is perpendicular to every row of A
practice.answer: Multiplying by A only stretches v, without turning it
practice.why: An eigenvector keeps its direction; the eigenvalue λ is the stretch factor.

practice.q: Which eigenvalue does plain power iteration find?
practice.answer: The one largest in size
practice.why: Repeated multiplication makes the part with the largest |λ| grow fastest until it dominates.

practice.q: What decides how fast power iteration converges?
options: The ratio of the second-largest eigenvalue to the largest
The length of the starting vector
How many zeros the matrix has
practice.answer: The ratio of the second-largest eigenvalue to the largest
practice.why: Each step shrinks the unwanted part by that ratio, so close eigenvalues mean slow progress.

practice.q: One multiplication of v = [1, 0] by A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. What does it print?
practice.why: Multiplying by [1, 0] picks out the first column of A, which is [2, 1].

lessons.title: The fast Fourier transform
lessons.summary: Taking a signal apart into the waves it is made of, in n log n steps.

sections.p: A sound, a day of temperatures or a row of pixels is a list of n samples. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) rewrites that list as a sum of waves: for each frequency k (k full cycles across the samples) it gives a complex number X(k) = Σj xj e−2πijk/n. Its size |X(k)| says how much of that wave is in the signal, and its angle says where the wave starts. This is how an equalizer shows bass and treble, how MP3 and JPEG decide what detail to drop, and how a tuner hears which note you play.

sections.h: From n² to n log n
sections.p: Computing every X(k) straight from the formula takes n multiplications for each of n frequencies: n² in all. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) notices that the transform of n samples can be built from the transforms of the even-numbered and the odd-numbered samples, each of size n/2, with one extra multiplication per pair. Splitting again and again down to single samples leaves log₂ n levels of n operations each. Gauss used the idea in 1805; James Cooley and John Tukey published it in 1965, and it became one of the most used algorithms in computing. For a million samples it is the difference between a trillion steps and twenty million:
sections.code:
print("     n    direct n*n    FFT n*log2(n)")
for p in [3, 10, 20]:
    n = 2 ** p
    print(f"{n:7d}  {n * n:14d}  {n * p:12d}")

sections.p: Instead of splitting recursively, the version below works in place. It first reorders the samples so that index i moves to the index whose binary digits are those of i backwards (with 16 samples, 0001 swaps with 1000); after that, the halves that the splitting would produce sit next to each other. Then it combines neighbours in pairs, pairs into fours, fours into eights, and so on. Each combining step, called a butterfly, takes two values u and t (the second already multiplied by a twiddle factor w = e−2πik/size) and replaces them by u + t and u − t. The signal is 1 + sin(2 cycles) + 0.5 cos(5 cycles), and the transform finds exactly those parts: 16 at k = 0 (the constant 1, added up 16 times), 8 at k = 2 and 4 at k = 5 (a wave of height A shows up as A·n/2).
sections.code:
import math

PI = math.acos(-1.0)


def fft(a):
    """Replace the list a (length a power of 2) by its discrete Fourier transform."""
    n = len(a)
    # 1. put the samples in bit-reversed order
    j = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        bit = n // 2
        while j & bit:
            j ^= bit
            bit //= 2
        j |= bit
        if i < j:
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    # 2. combine pairs, then fours, then eights, ... (butterflies)
    span = 2
    while span <= n:
        half = span // 2
        for start in range(0, n, span):
            for k in range(half):
                angle = -2 * PI * k / span
                w = complex(math.cos(angle), math.sin(angle))
                t = w * a[start + k + half]
                u = a[start + k]
                a[start + k] = u + t
                a[start + k + half] = u - t
        span *= 2


# 16 samples of 1 + sin(2 cycles) + 0.5 cos(5 cycles)
n = 16
x = [complex(1 + math.sin(2 * PI * 2 * j / n)
             + 0.5 * math.cos(2 * PI * 5 * j / n), 0) for j in range(n)]
fft(x)
print("  k      |X(k)|")
for k in range(n // 2 + 1):
    print(f"{k:3d}  {abs(x[k]):10.6f}")

sections.p: C99 has complex numbers built in through <complex.h>: double complex is the type, I is the imaginary unit, and cabs gives the size. The loops are the same as in Python.

Fortran has had a complex type since the 1960s, and arrays can start at 0 with a(0:), which keeps the index arithmetic the same as in C and Python. One trap: a variable called size would hide the built-in size function, so this version calls the block width span.
sections.code:
module fourier
  implicit none
contains
  ! Replace a (its size a power of 2) by its discrete Fourier transform.
  subroutine fft(a)
    complex(kind(1d0)), intent(inout) :: a(0:)
    complex(kind(1d0)) :: w, t, u, tmp
    double precision :: pi, angle
    integer :: n, i, j, bit, span, half, start, k
    pi = acos(-1d0)
    n = size(a)
    ! 1. put the samples in bit-reversed order
    j = 0
    do i = 1, n - 1
      bit = n / 2
      do while (iand(j, bit) /= 0)
        j = ieor(j, bit)
        bit = bit / 2
      end do
      j = ior(j, bit)
      if (i < j) then
        tmp = a(i)
        a(i) = a(j)
        a(j) = tmp
      end if
    end do
    ! 2. combine pairs, then fours, then eights, ... (butterflies)
    span = 2
    do while (span <= n)
      half = span / 2
      do start = 0, n - 1, span
        do k = 0, half - 1
          angle = -2 * pi * k / span
          w = cmplx(cos(angle), sin(angle), kind(1d0))
          t = w * a(start + k + half)
          u = a(start + k)
          a(start + k) = u + t
          a(start + k + half) = u - t
        end do
      end do
      span = span * 2
    end do
  end subroutine fft
end module fourier

program main
  use fourier
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 16
  complex(kind(1d0)) :: x(0:n-1)
  double precision :: pi
  integer :: j, k
  pi = acos(-1d0)
  ! 16 samples of 1 + sin(2 cycles) + 0.5 cos(5 cycles)
  do j = 0, n - 1
    x(j) = cmplx(1 + sin(2 * pi * 2 * j / n) + 0.5d0 * cos(2 * pi * 5 * j / n), 0d0, kind(1d0))
  end do
  call fft(x)
  print '(a)', '  k      |X(k)|'
  do k = 0, n / 2
    print '(i3, 2x, f10.6)', k, abs(x(k))
  end do
end program main

sections.p: In practice you call a library: numpy.fft in Python, or FFTW from C and Fortran, which handle any length (not only powers of 2) and real-valued input at half the cost. A few things to know when reading a spectrum: only frequencies up to n/2 can be told apart, and a wave faster than that aliases, showing up as a slower one, which is why audio is sampled at more than twice the highest pitch we hear. A wave that does not fit a whole number of cycles in the window leaks into neighbouring frequencies, so signals are often tapered at the ends first (a window function). The FFT also makes convolution fast, since convolving is just multiplying transforms, which speeds up blurring images, filtering sound and even multiplying huge integers.

practice.q: How many operations does the FFT need for n samples, compared with n² for the direct formula?
practice.answer: About n log₂ n
practice.why: There are log₂ n levels of splitting, each doing work proportional to n.

practice.q: A signal is 3 cos(4 cycles) sampled 32 times. What is |X(4)|?
practice.why: A wave of height A appears as A·n/2 = 3 × 32 / 2 = 48.

practice.q: With 16 samples, which index does 3 (binary 0011) swap with in the bit-reversal step?
practice.answer: 12 (binary 1100)
practice.why: Reading 0011 backwards gives 1100, which is 12.

practice.q: One butterfly with u = 3 and t = 1. What does it print?
practice.code:
u, t = 3, 1
print(u + t, u - t)
practice.why: A butterfly replaces the pair by their sum and their difference.
